newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - KLM earnings plunge, CEO to resign.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - KLM earnings plunge, CEO to resign.

text.p: KLM Royal Dutch Airlines said on Wednesday its profits fell sharply in 1996/97 as costs rose faster than revenues and the bottom line was hit by a hefty restructuring charge aimed at boosting future earnings.
KLM also unexpectedly announced its president and chief executive Pieter Bouw would stand down in August after six years at the helm to allow a colleague to oversee a crucial recovery plan.
Net profit for the year to March 31 fell to 236 million guilders ($125.2 million) from 547 million.
This included a pre-tax provision of 290 million guilders for the Focus 2000 restructuring programme which aims to boost operating profits by 1.5 billion guilders over three years.

But KLM said this was not the only factor behind the steep drop in earnings, noting that operating costs had risen by 13.1 percent while operating revenues rose only 8.6 percent -- thus continuing a trend which had already started in 1995/96.
Consequently operating profit, before the restructuring provision, fell to 89 million guilders from 453 million.
"This is a clear proof of the necessity for the new and substantial transformation process that has been initiated under the name Focus 2000," it said.
KLM said Bouw, 55, would resign as CEO at the annual meeting on August 5 and that its supervisory board planned to appoint chief operating officer Leo van Wijk, 50, to succeed him.

KLM said it regretted Bouw's decision but that after more than six years in charge of KLM, and at the dawn of a major restructuring programme, Bouw had felt the time was ripe for a transfer of leadership.

The Focus 2000 programme seeks a cumulative increase in KLM's operating profits of 1.5 billion guilders over the next three years, with two thirds coming from extra revenues and one third from a reduction in costs.
The slide in KLM's 1996/97 earnings came despite a higher contribution from its U.S. associate Northwest Airlines (NWA) of 442 million guilders versus 258 million in 1995/96.

This was mainly derived from the sale and revaluation of various types of NWA shares, but the fourth quarter also brought 59 million guilders in operational profits from Northwest following NWA's return to positive equity.
KLM said it expected 1997/98 operating income to show a significant improvement.
"On balance we expect for 1997/98 a significant improvement in operating income from the present unsatisfactory base," it said in a statement.
Its forecast was based on the assumption of a positive economic climate and a lower fuel price following a 29 percent increase in fuel costs in 1995/96.
Analysts were unimpressed by KLM's results, even though the bottom-line figure was close to their forecasts.
"At first, I thought these results were more or less in line (with expectations)," said Richard Brakenhoff of MeesPierson.

"However, if you look at the breakdown, operating profit was quite disappointing. That's offset by the contribution from Northwest Airlines. Some of the cost items were higher than expected," he said.
Nevertheless, KLM shares rose on the Amsterdam bourse, gaining 1.60 at 59.80.
Dealers attributed this to the news that Leo van Wijk, regarded as a wily strategist, was set to take over from Bouw.
